newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Orion Capital to stick to core.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Orion Capital to stick to core.

text.p: Orion Capital Corp plans to stick to its core, specialty lines of business and expand them through a combination of internal growth and selected acquisitions, the company's new chief executive said.

Marston Becker, who took the helm of Orion Capital on December 31, told Reuters in an interview that he believes the company's growth prospects are good and does not have any interest in diversifying into other lines.
"I think our best, near-term opportunities are adding to the lines we're already in," Becker said.

Orion Capital, which was formed in 1976 from the remains of the bankruptcy reorganization of Equity Funding Corp of America, operates workers compensation, professional liability, nonstandard auto, marine and specialty program businesses.
"All of those segments have nice continuing growth opportunities for us," he said.

"We probably will continue to emphasize the growth, both organically and through opportunistic acquisitions that align themselves with our existing lines of business and our existing operating companies."

That, he said, was how he expects the company to best meet its objectives of double digit revenue growth and 15 percent return on equity. Over each of the last eight years, the company achieved a return on average equity of 14 percent.
But, he said, the trick is finding acquisition candidates with competitive advantages that are fairly priced.
"That is a process of constantly looking and occasionally finding an opportunity," Becker said.
One such opportunity came in 1995, with the purchase of Wm. H. McGee & Co, a manager of marine insurance underwriting pools, from Sun Alliance Group Plc.

Orion Capital this year boosted its stake in Guaranty National Corp to about 80 percent from 49.5 percent and sold the ongoing business of its broker market reinsurance company SecurityRe Cos to The Hartford.
Becker said he does not plan to buy out the rest of Guaranty National that Orion does not already own.
Meanwhile, additional organic growth may come through further geographic expansion of those businesses which are still somewhat regional, he said.
The workers compensation business, for instance, has expanded into 12 new states over the last three years, but still operates in just a total of 24 states.
By helping clients to find ways to keep losses down, Orion Capital has managed to turn in better-than-average results in workers compensation despite the competitive environment, Becker said.

But, he said, he believes the workers compensation industry may be on the brink of a cycle in which insurers' reserves may be insufficient to pay the actual losses. That, he said, may discourage some of the competition.
"Frankly, that's a positive industry event," he said.
